Baby & Child

When your child is afraid of the dark

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

In daylight it is a coat on a peg. After the bedroom light goes out, the same shape looks like a person standing by the door. Ask your child to show you what they see from the pillow. Their answer can help you decide what to do tonight.

Find out what changes when the light goes out

Wait until your child is calm enough to talk. Ask what feels scary about the room at night. A younger child might point or draw a picture. An older one might describe a noise, an image from a programme, or worry about being too far away to call you. Some children cannot identify what started it.

Take a report about an actual person, noise or frightening event seriously and check on safety. When an ordinary object casts the shadow, look at it together with the light on. Move the coat if your child wants to. Once they recognise it, you can return to the bedtime story without a nightly search of the room.

Make a plan your child can count on tonight

Acknowledge how the room feels to them. You might say, “That shape looked different when we turned off the light. I’m here. Shall we put the coat on the chair?” One calm answer gives the child something they can understand. Teasing or arguing about how old they are can make it harder for them to tell you what they saw.

Choose a familiar order for getting into bed, such as washing, putting on pyjamas and reading one quiet story. A dim night-light can help the child recognise familiar shapes. If they worry about being alone, agree where you will sit or when you will come back. Make it a promise you can keep. If they wake frightened later, help them get their bearings and use the same plan.

Practise in the daytime

Ask your child to choose one thing they feel ready to try. They might close the curtains partway while you sit beside them and name three familiar objects they can still see. Another day they might try sitting in the same place with a little less light. Keep an easy way to turn the light back on.

Let them repeat a manageable step before increasing the challenge. If a step brings panic, make it smaller. Notice exactly what they managed, such as staying with you long enough to recognise the bookcase. A frightened child needs a chance to learn what the room is like at their own pace.

Choose stories and games that help

Ask which stories feel cosy and which ones leave an image behind after the book is closed. Save frightening programmes for another time. A story about a character who tries a small, brave step can give a child an idea to try in daylight. They can also invent their own ending.

A trial involving 68 children aged four to six tested a parent-led programme that combined a therapeutic book with a doll. The children had intense nighttime fears and avoided sleeping alone. Parents reported greater improvement with the programme than while waiting for treatment. Because the activities were tested together in this particular group, the study cannot tell families that any single book or toy will solve bedtime fears.

When bedtime fear takes over the day

Ask your child’s healthcare professional for help if fear regularly costs them sleep, leaves them too tired to learn or play, or spreads to daytime activities. It is also worth bringing up a marked change after a frightening event. The child’s account of what happened matters.

Bring an example of what they fear, what you tried and how the night went. A clinician can explore sleep, anxiety or the effect of a stressful experience and suggest support suited to the child. You can ask for help while continuing the bedtime routine they find reassuring.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask what is frightening and address genuine safety concerns.

Plan one manageable practice step with the child and repeat it when they are calm.

Seek advice for persistent fear, disrupted sleep or daytime avoidance.

How BeMama can help

BeMama uses the changing outline of a coat to show how a child can identify what frightened them and help choose a response.

When to seek help

If a child describes an actual threat or unsafe situation, take steps to keep them safe. Ask their healthcare professional for help if intense fear or sleep loss continues.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ask the child what looks or sounds different after the light goes out.
  • A dim light and a predictable check-in can help a child settle.
  • Practise an easier version of the scary situation together in daylight.
  • Describe repeated sleep loss or daytime avoidance to the child’s healthcare professional.

Frequently asked questions

What if my child can sleep only with someone beside them?

Ask what feels hardest when you leave. If being alone is the difficult part, agree on a gradual change together. You might start by sitting in a chair beside the bed and, when that feels manageable, move the chair a little farther away. Follow through on agreed check-ins.

What should I say if my child insists something is in the room?

Listen and check any real concern. If a shadow caused the fright, help the child recognise what casts it. Tell them you understand why it startled them. A brief explanation and a familiar bedtime activity can be easier to return to than repeated searches.

Is it okay to leave a light on?

Yes. A dim night-light that helps your child see the room and still fall asleep is a reasonable choice. Let them help choose where it goes. A bright screen playing a programme can add sounds or images that keep them alert.

How can I help them feel less afraid over time?

Choose one manageable activity together, such as looking at a familiar shelf in slightly dimmer light. Practise when your child is rested, praise the effort and agree on any next step. Persistent, severe fears deserve individual advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
